findings.title: Google token refresh stores the Zod SafeParse wrapper as the credential key
findings.body: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns the Zod safeParse result ({ success, data }), not the parsed data (parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts line 29). This line passes that wrapper directly to prisma.credential.update as `key`. With sync disabled (the default), every Google access-token refresh (about hourly) overwrites the stored key with `{ success: true, data: {...} }`, which has no top-level access_token, refresh_token or expiry_date. On the next GoogleCalendarService construction, googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key) fails in googleAuth, so Google Calendar breaks for every connected user. Other callers (zoomvideo, office365calendar, salesforce) read `.data` from the same helper, so this call site is inconsistent with them.

findings.title: prisma is used in the Salesforce CalendarService but never imported
findings.body: getClient now calls prisma.credential.update (line 96), but the file's imports (lines 1-20) do not include prisma from @calcom/prisma. This fails type-checking ('Cannot find name prisma') and throws a ReferenceError on every Salesforce connection, so the Salesforce calendar integration cannot be constructed.

findings.title: Zoho Bigin passes the credential id where refreshOAuthTokens expects the user id
findings.body: refreshAccessToken receives `credentialId` (the Cal.com credential primary key) and passes it as the third `userId` argument to refreshOAuthTokens. Every other provider passes credential.userId. With CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT enabled, the self-hoster endpoint is asked to refresh tokens for calcomUserId equal to a credential id, which is a different user. The returned tokens are then written into this user's credential, mixing accounts. The fix is to pass the user id (credential.userId) and keep the credential id only for the DB update.

findings.title: In sync mode refreshOAuthTokens returns a raw fetch Response that callers treat as provider data
findings.body: In the sync branch the helper returns the fetch Response without reading the body or checking response.ok. The non-sync branch returns a provider SDK or axios result, and callers read it with .data, .expiresIn or .data.error. With sync enabled these reads break: googlecalendar CalendarService.ts line 94 reads res?.data (undefined), so the TypeError is swallowed by the catch and Google tokens are never refreshed; hubspot CalendarService.ts line 192 derives expiryDate from expiresIn (undefined, giving NaN); zoho-bigin CalendarService.ts line 96 reads tokenInfo.data.error, which throws a TypeError that is not caught; zohocrm CalendarService.ts reads zohoCrmTokenInfo.data.error inside a try that silently logs. The helper should parse the body, check status, and return the same shape as the non-sync branch.

findings.title: In sync mode the HubSpot refresh writes a fetch Response object into the credential key
findings.body: In sync mode refreshOAuthTokens returns a fetch Response, so hubspotRefreshToken.expiresIn is undefined and expiryDate (line 192) becomes NaN. Line 198 then persists that Response object as the credential key. A Response has no token fields, so the stored key ends up with no access or refresh token (at most an expiryDate of null). If Prisma rejects the object instead, the refresh fails silently in the catch. Either way the HubSpot connection is never refreshed and its stored tokens are lost. The sync body must be parsed to JSON and the expiry derived before anything is persisted.

findings.title: A missing refresh_token is replaced with the literal string 'refresh_token' and persisted
findings.body: When the validated response has no refresh_token, this assigns the literal string 'refresh_token' and returns it as valid data. Callers persist it: office365calendar merges tokenResponse.data over the stored credential and zoomvideo sets key.refresh_token from it. In sync mode this always happens, because minimumTokenResponseSchema (lines 5-11) strips every field except access_token, so the real stored refresh token is overwritten with the placeholder. A later refresh (after sync is disabled, or for a provider that omits refresh_token) then fails with invalid_grant. The fallback should keep the existing refresh token rather than invent one.

findings.title: Schema selection here does not match the sync condition used in refreshOAuthTokens
findings.body: The minimal schema is selected when only the env vars are set. refreshOAuthTokens also requires a userId before calling the sync endpoint. So for team-owned credentials (userId null) on a sync-enabled instance, the provider's direct refresh response is validated with the minimal schema, which strips expires_in, expiry_date, refresh_token and instance_url. Google and Zoom then persist NaN or placeholder values. The schema choice should use the same condition as the branch that produced the response, or be passed in by the caller.

findings.title: minimumTokenResponseSchema's computed keys collapse to one key, so the expiry requirement is never enforced
findings.body: z.string().toString() returns the default '[object Object]' rather than a meaningful key name. Both computed properties (lines 8 and 10) therefore use the same key, and the second (z.unknown().optional()) overwrites the first. The intended rule 'any numeric property is the expiry' is not enforced, so a sync response containing only access_token passes validation with no expiry. The schema should name the expiry field explicitly (for example expiry_date) and validate it as a number.

findings.title: Zoom sync-mode refresh computes expiry_date from a field the minimal schema strips
findings.body: In sync mode parseRefreshTokenResponse validates with minimumTokenResponseSchema, which keeps only access_token, so expires_in is removed. newTokens.expires_in is therefore undefined, expiry_date becomes NaN, and it is persisted (serialized as null). The next getToken calls zoomTokenSchema.parse, which requires expiry_date to be a number, so the credential fails to parse and Zoom calls reject with 'Zoom credential keys parsing error' until the user reconnects.

findings.title: Zoom refresh sends appSlug 'zoomvideo' but the credential is stored under appId 'zoom'
findings.body: The Zoom callback creates credentials with appId 'zoom' (zoomvideo/api/callback.ts) and the installed-app path also uses slug 'zoom'. The sync request here sends appSlug 'zoomvideo', the directory name. A self-hoster's app store keyed by the Cal.com app slug will not find the app, or will find the wrong one, so Zoom sync refresh fails or returns the wrong credentials. The slug should match the stored appId.

findings.title: Webex sync response is validated against the full Webex schema, bypassing parseRefreshTokenResponse
findings.body: Zoom and Google route refreshed tokens through parseRefreshTokenResponse so the sync endpoint only needs to return an access token and expiry. Webex does not. This line validates against webexRefreshedTokenSchema, which requires an exact scope literal, token_type, refresh_token and refresh_token_expires_in. A sync endpoint following the documented contract (access token plus expiry) is always rejected with 'Invalid refreshed tokens were returned'. Also, expiry_date is only updated when expires_in is present (lines 103-105), so an endpoint that returns only an expiry never updates it. Webex should use the same helper as Zoom.

findings.title: Salesforce now refreshes its token on every client construction and bypasses the sync endpoint
findings.body: getClient runs from the constructor (line 57) and now always POSTs to login.salesforce.com and writes the credential row, even when the stored token is still valid. Every availability check, booking or list call that creates a service instance pays a network round trip and a DB write, and concurrent instances race on the same refresh token. Because this bypasses refreshOAuthTokens, Salesforce still calls Salesforce directly in sync mode, which defeats the PR's purpose. The statusText !== 'OK' check on line 86 is also unreliable (HTTP/2 responses have an empty statusText) and should check response.ok. Finally, the minimal schema applied to this direct response strips instance_url, so the stored key loses it when sync is enabled.

findings.title: Webhook credential update does not clear the invalid flag
findings.body: When a provider returns invalid_grant, the code sets credential.invalid = true (googlecalendar, webex, zoom and invalidateCredential). This handler replaces the key with freshly synced tokens but never resets invalid. A credential flagged invalid therefore stays invalid after the self-hoster pushes working tokens, and any code path that skips invalid credentials keeps skipping it. The update should also set invalid to false.

findings.title: findFirst-then-create lets concurrent webhook deliveries insert duplicate credentials
findings.body: The lookup (lines 62-70) and the create (line 83) are separate statements with no transaction or unique constraint covering (userId, appId). Two deliveries for the same user and app, such as a self-hoster retry, can both see no row and both insert. Later reads use findFirst and pick one row arbitrarily, so the app may keep using a stale token. The comment about upsert does not address this race. Wrap the lookup and write in a transaction, or enforce uniqueness at the database level.

findings.title: Malformed payloads and decryption failures escape as unhandled exceptions
findings.body: appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body) throws a ZodError on a bad body, and JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...)) (lines 57-59) throws on a wrong key or non-JSON plaintext. Neither is caught, so the caller gets an unstructured 500 rather than a 400 with a stable message. Use safeParse for a 400 response and wrap decryption and parsing in a try/catch.

findings.title: Webhook secret is compared with !== instead of a constant-time comparison
findings.body: The shared secret is compared with the !== operator, which short-circuits on the first mismatched character and can leak timing information about the secret. The route is the only authentication on an endpoint that writes decrypted third-party credentials, so use crypto.timingSafeEqual (hashing both sides first so lengths match).

findings.title: Refresh replaces the whole credential key with the raw refresh response
findings.body: The stored key is overwritten with responseBody. In sync mode that response is the self-hoster's minimal payload (access token and expiry, per the comment in refreshOAuthTokens), so refresh_token and other stored fields are dropped from the credential. A later non-sync refresh then has no refresh token to use. The new fields should be merged into the existing key, as the Zoom and Google paths do.

findings.title: isTokenValid is inverted, so expired tokens are never refreshed and valid ones always are
findings.body: isTokenValid returns true when token.expiryDate < Date.now(), meaning the token is expired. getToken then does isTokenValid(...) ? resolve() : refreshAccessToken(...), so an expired token skips refresh and the stale access token is used, while a still-valid token triggers a refresh on every call. This is the path the PR wraps in refreshOAuthTokens. Also, line 219 stores expiryDate as Date.now() + 60 * 60, which is 3.6 seconds in milliseconds, so the stored expiry is wrong as well. The pre-existing defect is in code this PR modifies and should be fixed alongside it.

findings.title: Sync request carries no authentication and its response is not status-checked
findings.body: The outbound POST to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT sends only calcomUserId and appSlug, with no shared secret or signature, so the endpoint cannot verify that the request came from this instance. The reply is then trusted to overwrite stored tokens. There is no timeout and no response.ok check, so an error page or a stalled endpoint is handled as a token response. The inbound webhook already uses a shared secret, so the outbound call should send one too, with a timeout and a status check.

findings.title: New credential sync and refresh paths are shipped without tests
findings.body: The PR checklist states that no tests were added. The new endpoint (secret check, decryption, create/update logic) and the shared helpers (refreshOAuthTokens, parseRefreshTokenResponse) have no unit tests. Defects in this PR, including the SafeParse wrapper stored as a key, a Response treated as token data, the placeholder refresh token, and the zoho-bigin user id mix-up, are the kind that tests of the helpers' return values and the sync branch would catch. At minimum add tests for refreshOAuthTokens in both modes and for parseRefreshTokenResponse's return shape.
